summary: in the Civil Appeal No. 10480/2023 dated 23.9.2024 (‘SC Order’), the present matter needs to be referred to the arbitration by the Commission. On the contrary, the Respondents in the matter have vehemently contested such averments of the Petitioner. Subsequently, both sides were permitted to file their respective submissions on the above aspect and were extensively heard, as noted below. 3. Learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that since the primary issue in the matter pertains to the validity of the Power Purchase Agreement dated 24.12.2021, the matter requires arbitration in light of the DVC judgment as well as the SC Order. Learned senior counsel for the Respondent TPL submitted that there is no arbitration agreement between the Petitioner and TPL, and in the absence thereof, no reference can be made to the arbitrator. Learned senior counsel further submitted that while there is an arbitration clause in the agreement entered into between the Respondents, TPL, and PTC, PTC has entered into the said agreement in the capacity of a merchant trader. In fact, the Petitioner's various prayers relate only to the Agreement entered into by the Petitioner with PTC. After considering the submissions of the parties, the parties were directed to file their notes of arguments on the aspect of arbitrability of the dispute. 4. Pursuant to the directions of the Commission issued _vide_ Record of Proceedings dated 11.2.2025, the Petitioner and the Respondents, PTC and TPL, have filed their respective submissions on the aspect of arbitrability of the dispute in the Petition. concluded their respective arguments on the arbitrability of the dispute involved in the matter. After hearing both sides, the Commission reserved the matter for order on the arbitrability of the disputes. Further, the Commission directed the parties to file their respective written submissions/ notes of argument in the matter. The Petitioner and the Respondents have filed their respective written submissions on the aspect of arbitrability of the dispute(s). The gist of the submissions of the parties is as under: (iii) In the DVC judgment, the APTEL itself divided the reliefs sought thereunder to identify a ‘main issue’, i.e., the issue of termination of the PPA, which it held to be a non-tariff issue. The Cause of Action in the present Petition has not sought to be split by the Petitioner, but the Commission ought to identify that the primary relief sought by the Petitioner pertains to whether the PPA is a valid document or not. Since the primary issue pertains to the validity of the PPAs entered into between the parties and does not relate to tariff or regulation of tariff, the same ought to be referred to arbitration. 7. The Respondent TPL has submitted on the aspect of arbitrability of the dispute in question as under: (x) The prayers of the Petitioner reveal that the primary dispute relates to compensation for the amounts charged by the PTC on account of diversion of power supply by the Petitioner. The Petitioner has sought to be exempted from paying such compensation and sought a declaration of certain events as change in law. The same falls directly within the category of tariff disputes set out in the DVC judgment. In the present case, there is no relief sought by the Petitioner against TPL. (xii) The dispute involved in the matter is not arbitrable under the A&C Act in view of the several parties involved in the matter. In adjudication, disputes involving several parties can be heard and decided in one petition. However, there will be several arbitrations if the dispute is to be referred to arbitration under each PPA separately and decided separately, with the possibility of conflicting decisions. 8. We have considered the submissions made by the parties and perused the documents made available on record. The primary issue that arises for our consideration is whether the disputes involved in this case are, as explained in the DVC Judgment, tariff disputes or non-tariff disputes? Further, both sides have also raised certain additional issues, such as the existence/ non-existence of an arbitration agreement between the Petitioner and TPL, the stage at which an arbitration can be invoked/ compliance with Section 8 of the A & C Act 1996, the scope and meaning of the term “ _Mutatis Mutandis_ ”, etc., as noted above. However, the need to examine these issues would arise only once we conclude that the disputes in the matter are non-tariff and are mandatorily required to be referred to arbitration. Hence, these issues will be addressed in the latter part of the order, if so required. 12. It is true that the Petitioner, at Paragraph 97(a), has also prayed for a declaration that the MB Power PPA is not in conformity with the MoP Short-Term Guidelines and GERC Guidelines. However, this prayer alone cannot dictate the nature of the primary disputes as sought to be argued by the Petitioner. It is not the case of the Petitioner that the rest of the prayers/grounds are mere alternatives to the above principal prayer/ground. In any case, whether or not the MB Power PPA conforms to the MoP and GERC Guidelines, and the consequences are not simpliciter disputes arising out of the contractual arrangement between the parties. Where the Guidelines vest the power to approve any deviations therefrom in the Commission, the Commission would also have the necessary power to examine the dispute arising from the alleged noncompliance with/deviations from the Guidelines and the effects/ consequences of such non-compliance/deviation.
